candidate.answerReason: The probability is \(W(p)=10p^3(1-p)^2\). One solution is \(p=2/5\); continuity guarantees another between \(3/5\) and \(4/5\), because the target lies strictly between the probabilities at those endpoints.

methods.label: Show that two probabilities are possible
methods.explanation:
Finding one value of \(p\) does not establish that it is the only one. We will first write the probability as a function of \(p\), then show that it takes the required value at two different inputs.

A sequence with exactly three heads is determined uniquely by its two tail positions. There are \(5\cdot4/2=10\) choices: the ordered count \(5\cdot4\) counts each pair of positions twice. By independence, each such sequence has probability \(p^3(1-p)^2\). The ten sequences are disjoint, so
\[
W(p)=10p^3(1-p)^2,\qquad 0\le p\le1.
\]
Substitution gives
\[
W\left(\frac25\right)
=10\left(\frac25\right)^3\left(\frac35\right)^2
=\frac{144}{625}.
\]
Thus \(p=2/5\) is one possibility. To establish a second, calculate
\[
W\left(\frac35\right)=\frac{216}{625},
\qquad
W\left(\frac45\right)=\frac{128}{625}.
\]
The target \(144/625\) lies strictly between these two values. Since \(W\) is a polynomial, it is continuous on \([3/5,4/5]\), so it must equal the target at some point strictly inside that interval.

This second value is different from \(2/5\); both values also describe unfair coins. Therefore \(\boxed{p\text{ is not uniquely determined}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
